Vs.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 27th November 1984 passed by the High Court Division, Chittagong Bench in Second Appeal No. 279 of 1973).
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J : This appeal by leave is against judgment and decree dated 27-11-1984 passed by the High Court Division, Chittagong Division in Second Appeal No. 279 of 1973 allowing the appeal setting aside those dated 9-3-1973 of the District Judge, Chittagong in Title Appeal No. 149 of 1971 affirming those dated 5-5-1971 of the Munsif, Second Court, Patiya in Title Suit No. 85 of 1959.

2. The appellants as the plaintiffs filed the suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession or in the alternative for recovery of possession if found to be out of possession stating, inter alia, that the suit land comprising of Schedules 1 and 2 recorded in CS Khatian No. 2 and 2A originally belonged to one Baisnab Chandra Dey who was succeeded by son Abhoy Charan Dey. After the death of Abhoy Charan Dey his son Ananda inherited the same. But Ananda being the minor boy possessed the same through his maternal uncle one Jogesh Chandra Dey. Thereafter for legal necessity and maintenance of minor Ananda his uncle transferred the land to the predecessor of the plaintiffs by a kabala Exhibit 1 dated 7-12-1926. Since then the plaintiffs were in exclusive possession of the suit land. The plaintiffs also purchased some land situated to the western side of Schedule 1 property from the principal defendants and predecessors of other defendants by a registered kabala on 20-11-1930. The proforma defendant No. 8 Ananda after attaining majority affirmed the aforesaid sale of the suit land. During the PS operation Ram Kumar, the maternal uncle of Abhoy Charan Dey fraudulently got schedule 2 land recorded in his name. Since the defendants threatened to dispossess, the plaintiff instituted the suit.

3. The suit was decreed by the trial Court and an appeal therefrom was dismissed. The respondents thereafter moved the High Court Division in Second Appeal and the appeal was allowed dismissing the suit. Previously the matter went up to the High Court Division in Second Appeal No. 462 of 1964 and then the suit was remanded to the lower Appellate Court on 27-11-1968 for re-hearing and disposal of appeal on the evidence on record. After remand both the parties filed the compromise petition to allow the appeal with direction to remand the case to the trial Court to enable the parties to prove certain documentary evidence and accordingly the suit was remanded to the trial Court. Thereafter, the trial Court again  decreed the suit which was affirmed by the Court of appeal below, against which the defendants preferred Second Appeal No. 279 of 1973 and the appeal was allowed on 27-11-1984 against which' the present appeal arose by way of a leave to appeal.

4. Leave was granted to consider the submission made by Moulvi Md Wahidullah that both the trial Court and the lower Appellate Court correctly considered the question of adverse possession on the basis of the evidence that was led by the respective parties in the case, inasmuch as the Courts below found that Baishnab, the admitted original owner of the suit land, was in possession for more than 12 years before the institution of the suit and on that basis correctly held that the plaintiff had acquired valid title by adverse possession in the suit land. According to the learned Advocate, this finding of fact with regard to adverse possession has been wrongly misconstrued by the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division and, on that view, wrongly dismissed the suit. The learned Advocate further submits that concurrent findings of fact as to possession of the plaintiff for more than 12 years has been wrongly set aside in second appeal which does not suffer from any illegality or defect in procedure.

5. On perusal of the judgment of the trial Court it appears that the trial Court found that CS Khatians Exhibits 2 and 2(a) stand in the name of Baishnab Charan Dey original raiyat in respect of the suit land on the basis of an oral Bandabasti and that the defendant could not prove that the suit land belonged to Jituram. The defendant though sought to allege an unregistered Muktinama (Annexure-C) executed by Ananda but the trial Court on evidence found that all person concerned wrote in the Muktinama with the same pen and ink whereas the body of the same shows otherwise and would lead a prudent person to believe that it is a fabricated document. The trial Court also believed that during the minority of Ananda the burden of recording the suit land was with Jituram who had fraudulently entered his name as there was nothing on record to show that the suit land originally belonged to Jituram. The trial Court also found that Ram Kumar, maternal uncle of Abhoy Charan fraudulently got Schedule 2 recorded in his name.

6. As regards possession, the trial Court found that the plaintiffs paid rent of the suit land through defendant and Exhibit B series also shows that Baisnab was raiyat of the suit land. The trial Court also arrived at a finding of fact based on material on record that the suit land was in possession of the plaintiffs and that the suit is not barred by limitation.

7. The Court of appeal below found that the schedule 1 land recorded in CS (Khasra) Khatian No. 267 (Exhibit 2A) and the schedule 2 land recorded in CS (Khasra) Khatian No. 260 in the name of Baisnab in raiyat right was taken lease from one Ram Krishna Chowdhury and others and that the defendants could not acquire any title or possession of the suit land in schedule 2 recorded in the name of Ram Krishna in RS Khatian No. 239 Exhibit D 1 and in the name of Nikunja and others in PS Khatian No. 185 Exhibit E(1) as no basis could be shown for such recording. In view of the plaintiff's case that during RS Khatian Ram Kumar, maternal uncle of Abhoy Charan, fraudulently got schedule 2 land recorded in his name, the Court of appeal below on consideration of evidence on record arrived at a finding of fact that "RS Khatian 239 in the name of Ram Kumar Exhibit D(1) and RS Khatian 185 Exhibit D and the PS Khatian Exhibit E(1) in the name of Ram Kumar and Nikunja and others are fabricated documents and cannot be accepted as genuine as they had no basis to be so recorded." Similarly, "PS Khatian 23 Exhibit E(2) in the name of Niranjan, Nikunja and others has no basis at all as admittedly the RS Khatian 17 Exhibit 3 was prepared in the name of Ananda under the supervision of Ram Kumar and there is no basis for the preparation of PS Khatian 23 Exhibit E(2) in the name of Nikunja and others in respect of schedule 1 land." The Court of appeal below concurred with the trial Court as regards Exhibit C Muktinama which could not confer the defendant with any title in respect of the suit property. The Court of appeal below also did not find the suit land originally possessed by Baisnab was succeeded by his son Abhoy Charan and Anancla and thus Jituram or his successive heirs have any interest nor had possession in the suit land. Apart from PWs supporting the possession of the plaintiffs DW 1 Niranjan himself admitted the possession of the plaintiffs.

8. The Court of appeal below also held that "Ananda @ Ananga being the sole owner of the disputed properties was the only competent man to transfer the property to anybody he liked and the plaintiff's case is that Jogendra, the maternal uncle of Ananda @ Ananga, transferred the disputed properties to the plaintiffs Jiban Krishna Dey by kabala Exhibit 1 dated 7-12-1926 appears to be true." The Court of appeal below also found the possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land. DW 1 Niranjan himself admitted that by kabala purchase of some land from them PW 1 became a co-sharer with them in respect of the bhiti land. The Court of appeal below further arrived at a finding that it was admitted by both the parties that this kabala Exhibit 1 did not confer any title to the plaintiffs in respect of the disputed properties, as the same was executed by Jogendra, the maternal uncle of Ananda, without showing that he was executing the same for and on behalf of the minor Ananda @ Ananga as his guardian. The kabala executed by Jogendra has been proved but Jogendra did not execute the kabala as the guardian of the minor. The plaintiffs did not acquire the title in respect of the property concerned though they are in possession since 1926 and on consideration of the materials on record the court of appeal below held that since the plaintiffs are in possession of the disputed land for more than 12 years before the institution of the suit, thus acquired title in respect of the suit property by adverse possession against the defendants and all others. The Court of appeal below also found that the plaintiffs paid rent though the defendants by Exhibits Band B2 and B3 and found the Exhibit B4 and B5 are fabricated documents and accordingly, the Court of appeal below affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court. The High Court Division, however, assessed the evidence of the parties afresh and dismissed the suit reversing the findings of fact arrived at by the Courts below and held that the plaintiffs have failed to prove their Case of adverse possession for which they are not entitled to any decree or declaration of title and confirmation of possession.

9. Mr Abdus Salam Khan, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellant, has assailed the impugned judgment submitting that the High Court was incompetent to disturb the finding of fact arrived at by the final Court of fact on consideration of evidence on record inasmuch as it erred in law in disturbing the finding as to adverse possession arrived at on the basis of the evidence and that disturbing the finding of fact arrived at by the Courts below that the Baisnab admitted that the original owner was in possession and the possession of the suit land was correctly recorded in his name in CS Khatian and that the plaintiffs also acquired right by adverse possession on the basis of the purchase from Jogendra maternal uncle of Ananda and that the Courts below on consideration of evidence on record found that the record of schedule 2 land in RS in the name of Ram Kumar and subsequent PS Khatian has no basis and accordingly, erred in law in disturbing the concurrent finding of fact based on evidence on record arrived at by the Courts below.

10. Mr Sharifuddin Chaklader, the learned Advocate-on-Record appearing for the respondents, submitted that the said schedule 2 having been recorded in the name of Ram Kumar in the RS Khatian who is son of Jitu Ram, the owner of the suit land but part of the land recorded in the name of domesticated son-in-law did not acquire any right, title and possession. The learned Advocate-on-Record further submitted that in the absence of any issue as to adverse possession the Court of appeal below erred in law in holding that the plaintiffs have acquired title on the basis of adverse possession.

11. Admittedly the land in suit of the schedules were recorded in the name of Baisnab in CS (Khasra) Khatian No. 267 (Exhibit 2A) and CS . (Khasra) Khatian No. 260. The plaintiffs have led evidence to show that the, suit land so recorded belonged to Baisnab Chandra Dey who has acquired raiyat right taking lease from the landlord Ram Krishna Chowdhury and others and the tenancy in (Nal land) Exhibit 2 has been taken lease by Baisnab from Khas Mahal, Patiya at a rental of Rs 1/4 and the Empress of India the rent free tenancy in schedule recorded in Exhibit 2(a) (Bhiti land) in raiyati right was taken lease of by Baisnab from one Ram Krishna Charan and others. The presumption of the CS Khatian under section 103(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act is that every entry in a record of rights finally published shall be the evidence of the matter referred to in such entry and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved to be incorrect. Reference may be made in this regard to the case of Akrab Ali and others vs Zahiruddin Kari and others. 30 DLR (SC) 81.

12. The respondents claimed that settlement Khatians namely, RS and PS Khatians have been made in the name of Ramkumar and in the name of his heirs on succession. The plaintiffs had no interest in the suit land far less possession therein referring to RS Khatian No. 239 Exhibit D(I), RS Khatian Exhibit D in the name of Nikunja and others and RS Khatian 185 Exhibit E(I) in the name of Nikunja and others but the defendants could not produce any basis of the said recording so as to nullify the entries in CS Khatian and in the absence. of any evidence on record to show that either Ramkumar or Nikunja became the owner of the property recorded in CS Khatian Exhibit 2 or there was any settlement by the landlords in the name of Nikunja or Ramkumar. The learned District Judge being the final court of fact on consideration of the evidence on record concurrently arrived at the finding of fact that RS Khatian 239 in name of Ramkumar, Exhibit D(I) and RS Khatian 185 Exhibit D and the PS Khatian Exhibit E (I) in the name of Ramkumar and Nikunja and others are fabricated documents and cannot be accepted as they had no basis to be so recorded. Similarly, RS Khatian No. 17 Exhibit 3 in the name of Ananda in respect of schedule 1 land and corresponding PS Khatian 23 Exhibit E (2) in the name of Nikunja and others had no basis at all as admittedly RS Khatian 17 Exhibit 3 was prepared in the name of Ananga under the supervision of Ram Kumar without any basis.

13. The trial Court found that the Muktinama Exhibit C was a fabricated and forged document prepared for the purpose of the suit and the court of appeal below observed that the defendants gave a go-bye to Exhibit C to prove his case. Thus, there is no basis for PS Khatian Exhibit E2. Exhibit 1 is the kabala by Jogendra, maternal uncle of Ananga which was ratified by Ananga, attaining majority as he did never claim the property back from the plaintiffs.

14. The Court of appeal below also concurred with the finding as to possession holding that the conduct of the defendants in having Exhibit C from Ananga and the evidence of PW 1 read with those of PWs 2 and 3 show that the suit land originally possessed by Baisnab who was succeeded by his son Abhoy Charan and then by minor son Ananga and thus Jitendra or his heir had no interest in the suit land nor they possessed the same. DW 1 Niranjan also admitted the plaintiff as the co-sharers with them in the Bhiti land.

15. Though kabala Exhibit, 1 did not admittedly confer any title upon the plaintiff in respect of the disputed properties and it is established that Jogendra sold the disputed property to plaintiffs on the basis of kabala Exhibit 1 and the plaintiffs did not acquire any title in respect of the property but since the plaintiffs have been able to prove possession since 1926 duly corroborated by PWs 2 & 3, the Court of appeal below disbelieving the evidence of DWs as to defendant's possession arrived at the finding of fact that the plaintiffs were in possession of the suit land for more than 12 years before the institution of the suit and thus perfected their title in respect of the suit land by adverse possession against the defendants and others.

16. The Court of Appeal below also held that Exhibits (4) & (5) the rent receipts showing Ramkumar as tenant for the year 1288 and 1289 Moghi Era are forged and fabricated and that nonpayment of the rent by the plaintiffs predecessor or plaintiffs did not extinguish their right in the suit  land.

17. The High Court Division, however, proceeded to consider the evidence of the parties afresh holding that "since I am disposing of the appeal invoking the power under section 103 CPC let me discuss the evidence of the witnesses adduced by the parties" and accordingly, assessed the evidence afresh and while disbelieving the evidence of PWs relating to the possession of the plaintiffs and their maternal uncle Jogendra in the suit land, found favour with the evidence of the DWs. The High Court Division also relied in the recital of Exhibit C.

18. Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure authorises the High Court Division to interfere with the finding of fact if there is any error of law or procedure affecting merit of the case. In the instant case the Court of appeal below has arrived at the finding regarding title of the plaintiffs by way of adverse possession. Paragraph 4 of the plaint specifically asserted that:

৪। ৮ নং মোঃ বিবাদীর ভরণ পোষণ ও উপরিস্থ জমিদারের কর ইত্যাদি আদায় করার বৈধ প্রয়োজনে ৮ নং মোঃ বিবাদীর স্বার্থে ও হিতার্থে ৮ নং মোঃ বিবাদীর অভিভাবক স্বরূপে তদীয় মাতুল পার্শ্বলিপি ব্যক্তি উচিৎ মূল্যে ১/২  নং তপসিলের বর্ণিত জমি বাদীর নিকট নির্দয় সাফ বিক্রি করায় বাদী তফসিলের বর্ণিত জমিতে ৮ নং মোঃ বিবাদীর যাবতীয় স্বত্বে স্বত্ববান হইয়া তাহাতে তামাদির উর্ধ্বকাল যাবত খাস দখলদার ও কালগুজার আছি । উক্ত মতে বাদী উভয় তপসিলের বর্নিত জমিতে তামাদি দখল ও স্বত্ব অর্জন করিয়াছে।

The plaintiff also prayed for relief, inter alia, that:

(ক) বিরোধীয় ১/২ নং তপশীলের বর্নিত জমিতে বাদীর খরিদা রায়তী ও আদি দখল  সাব্যস্তে তাহাতে বাদীর দখল স্থিরতর থাকায় ডিক্রি হয়।

19. In the light of the averments and prayer as aforesaid in the plaint after remand an issue was framed as to whether the plaintiffs have acquired any right by way of adverse possession and evidence in the suit was led and accordingly, the Court of appeal below on consideration of evidence on record held that in view of the possession of the plaintiffs since 1926 and that Jogendra did not transfer the property for and on behalf of Ananda, the minor and thus the transfer was invalid one and that it is proved on admitted evidence that the plaintiffs are in possession of the disputed properties for more than 12 years before the institution of the suit and that Baisnab was in possession all along and that the plaintiffs were in possession on the date of filing of the suit and was also in possession for more than 12 years before the institution of the suit and thus perfected their title in respect of the suit properties by adverse possession against the defendants and all others.

20. In the case of Mir Laik Ali vs Standard Vacuum Oil Company (ESSO) and Abdur Razzak reported in 16 DLR (SC) 287 it has been held inter alia that:

"When there is an invalid transfer in favour of a person and he holds possession of the property in his own right and adverse to the transferor. It he continues in possession of immovable property for more than twelve years he will acquire an indefeasible title."

21. The said finding as to adverse possession has basis in pleading and evidence on record and accordingly, could not be disturbed in the second appeal. In the aforementioned decision in 30 DLR (SC) 81 it was held that the High Court Division was not competent to interfere with finding of fact arrived at by the lower Appellate Court which is based on appreciation of evidence, however wrong the same may appear in the absence of error of law or procedure, affecting merit of the case.

22. Similar view has been expressed in the case of Madan Gopal & ors vs Maran Bepari & ors reported in 21 DLR (SC) 448 wherein it has been held that:

"The legal position does not admit of any doubt that a concurrent finding of fact reached by the lower courts will not be disturbed by the High Court in a second appeal even if it disagrees with that finding on its own view of the evidence although the concurrent finding of the lower courts may appear to be grossly erroneous, unless, as laid down in sub-section (c) of section 100, the error or defect discovered is of a substantial character pertaining to the procedure as provided by the Code or by any other law for the time being in force which may possibly have produced an error or defect in the decision of the case upon its merits. Interference would also be justified if the decision of the lower courts is found to be contrary to law or some usage having the force of law or has failed to determine some material issue of law or usage having the force of law."

23. In view of the concurrent findings of fact based on evidence on record arrived at by the Court of appeal below affirming those of the trial Court. The High Court Division acted illegally in disturbing those findings of fact, assessing himself the evidence on record in the absence of error of law or procedure affecting merit of the case. Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not authorise the High Court Division to disturb the finding of fact of the Court of appeal below, the final Court of fact, arrived at on appreciation of the evidence even though the High Court Division does not agree with the finding arrived at by the Court of appeal below on consideration of the evidence on record.

<u>24. Thus the High Court Division exceeded its jurisdiction conferred under section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure in disturbing the concurrent findings of fact arrived at by the Courts below in the absence of any misreading or non-consideration of evidence or any error of law or procedure affecting the merit of the case.</u>

<u>The result is, therefore, this appeal is allowed with costs. The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division are set aside and those of the learned District Judge duly affirming those of the learned Munsif are restored.</u>

End.
